chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Ali ibn Muhammad, from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Suleiman ibn Dawud Al-Minqari, from Ali ibn Hashim ibn Al-Barid, from his father, that a man asked Ali ibn Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) about asceticism, so he said:

(It is) ten things. The highest degree of asceticism is the lowest degree of piety, and the highest degree of piety is the lowest degree of conviction, and the highest degree of conviction is the lowest degree of satisfaction.
Indeed, asceticism is in a verse from the Book of Allah, the Exalted, 'So that you may not despair over what has escaped you, nor be happy at what He has given you.'

key_terms.الرِّضَا: Satisfaction or contentment with divine decree
key_terms.الزُّهْد: Asceticism or detachment from the world
key_terms.الْوَرَع: Piety or God-consciousness in avoiding doubtful matters
key_terms.لِكَيْلا تَأْسَوْا: So that you may not despair

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual hierarchy of asceticism in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam Ali ibn Al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin) outlines a spiritual hierarchy where asceticism (zuhd) serves as the foundation for piety (wara'), which in turn leads to conviction (yaqin) and ultimate satisfaction (rida). This hadith, recorded in al-Kafi, emphasizes that true zuhd is not merely material renunciation but an internal state of emotional balance, explicitly linked to the Quranic verse in Surah Al-Hadid regarding not grieving over lost blessings nor rejoicing over gained ones. This framework illustrates the Shia understanding of spiritual progression from external discipline to internal tranquility.
